chunks.text: Prosopis cineraria belongs to the pea family Fabaceae (mimosoid clade), with synonyms including Mimosa cineraria and Prosopis spicigera. It is native to arid Western Asia and the Indian subcontinent — Afghanistan, Bahrain, Iran, India, Oman, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Yemen — and has also become established as an introduced species in parts of Southeast Asia such as Indonesia. It is a modest tree, usually 3–5 m tall, with bipinnate leaves of seven to fourteen leaflets across one to three pinnae, thorny internodes, small creamy-yellow flower clusters, and seed pods. It is exceptionally drought-hardy, tolerating annual rainfall as low as 15 cm and thriving in highly alkaline and saline soils, which makes it an indicator species for deep water tables in desert landscapes.

In the Thar Desert region, the tree's pods (called sangri or singhri) are a traditional food, cooked into curries and kadhi, and form part of the well-known Rajasthani dish 'panchkuta'. The tree's deep roots and tolerance of extreme aridity make it a key tool against desertification, and the UAE — where khejri is the national tree — runs a 'Give a Ghaf' campaign encouraging citizens to plant it in home gardens. The famous 'Tree of Life' in Bahrain, roughly 400 years old and growing in the desert with no apparent water source, is a Prosopis cineraria.

The khejri is central to one of India's founding environmental events: in 1730 at the village of Khejarli near Jodhpur, Maharaja Abhai Singh's men were sent to fell khejri trees for palace construction. Amrita Devi and her three daughters gave their lives hugging the trees in protest, and the ensuing resistance is said to have cost 363 lives — a sacrifice that directly inspired the Chipko movement of the 1970s. The tree is the state tree of both Rajasthan (as khejri) and Telangana (as jammi). It also carries deep religious meaning in Hinduism, especially around Dussehra/Vijayadashami, and the Mahabharata describes the Pandavas hiding their weapons in a khejri tree during their year of exile before retrieving and worshipping it. In Tamil Sangam literature it appears as the 'Vanni' tree, symbolising sacred assembly and truth.
